newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION-LIMITED BUDGET OPTIONS FOR INDIA GOVT-LLOYDS.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-LIMITED BUDGET OPTIONS FOR INDIA GOVT-LLOYDS.

text.p: The following are excerpts from an executive summary of a pre-budget analysis by Bombay-based Lloyds Securities.
With a coalition government, consisting of various parties pulling in different directions, the finance minister may not be able to do much with the coming budget.
The gameplan will be to boost lthe mutually agreed areas like infrastructure and avoid sensitive decisions like privatisastion of the insurance sector.
+ Further rationalisation/reduction in tariff may not be possible:
Budgets over the past five years have attempted to rationalise and reduce the tariff structure to make the domestic economy globally competitive.
Since most of the rates of duties are close to the levels suggested by the tax reforms committee, substantial reductions, save for a few products, is unlikely.
+ No major indirect tax reductions likely:

Looking at the current economic scenario, it is quite likely that no major custom tariff reductions would be made but a moderate reduction in domestic tariff is possible to kick start the economy and specific industry segments.
+ Further policy issues regarding infrastructure:

The paucity of infrastructure in the country will force the government to focus on policy changes pertaining to this sector. The India Infrastructure Report would form the basis for the change. Issues relating to funding of infrastructure projects will be addressed.
Long-term funding institutions like provident funds, pension funds and insurance companies may be allowed to invest a part of their corpus in infrastructure funds.
Incentives by way of income tax exemption on dividend from infrastructure companies and increased FII investment limits, may also be seen in the budget.
+ Surcharge on corporate tax:
Hike in administered product prices likely:

A railway tariff hike is likely. The biggest imponderable is the inevitable fuel price hike. If the government postpones it, the intensity of a hike later would be more severe. The government might soften the hike by reducing duties on crude imports and cess on domestic production which will translate into a higher fiscal deficit.
+ Restructuring telecom tariffs:
An upward revision cannot be ruled out, except for the international tariffs which is a sensitive area subsequent to the signining of WTO and VSNLl's proposed GDR issue.
+ Fiscal deficit in 1997/98 may be targeted at 5.0 pct of GDP though we do not expect the same to be achieved:

This target may be achieved through a moderate growth in revenue mobilisation of 13-15 percent and a lower expenditure growth of 12-13 percent. The economic growth is estimated at 6.5 percent per annum.

These estimates would however be difficult to achieve as expenditure management would be a tough task. There will be lower revenue mobilisation due to lower domestic output in FY98 (than is estimated). For current year too, the government was targeting a fiscal deficit of 5.0 percent which is unrealistic.
+ Pressure on corporate profitability may continue:

With no major tariff changes expected and input costs (especially power, fuel and freight) increasing, the pressure on corporate profitability is expected to continue especially for commodity players sensitive to these inputs. Demand-led growth is also unlikely in the immediate aftermath of the budget.
Major growth impetus to corporate profitability can be seen only as economic cycle picks up and commodity prices recover.
+ Markets sensitive to a few broad set of proposals:
Stocks markets in the immediate run after the budget are sensitive to a few broad proposals.

If markets move up on increased expectations of policy proposals in the run upto the budget, it is quite likely that the budget will find it difficult to satisfy these expectations as it has to operate in a set fiscal ambit governed by the political coalition.
In such a scenario, price movements subsequent to the budget are expected to be rather subdued and the stock price rally before the budget could be lused to book profits.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
